def: Relating to the serosa, the outer serous membrane lining body cavities and covering organs. Tumor invasion through the serosal surface indicates deeper spread of cancer.
A red patch on a mucous membrane that cannot be classified as any other disease, with a high risk of dysplasia or carcinoma. On the glans penis it is called erythroplasia of Queyrat.
A network of veins around the spermatic cord that drains the testis and cools arterial blood. Dilation of it causes a varicocele.
A CDK4/6 inhibitor that blocks cell-cycle progression through the Rb phosphorylation step, used with endocrine therapy in ER-positive breast cancer.
The peritoneal fold carrying the ovarian vessels from the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall. The ureter lies close to it, so it is at risk during ovarian surgery.
A pregnancy lasting 42 weeks or more, increasing risk of meconium aspiration, macrosomia and stillbirth.
An enzyme that unwinds double-stranded DNA at the replication fork by breaking hydrogen bonds between base pairs.
A laboratory technique that transfers separated molecules from a gel onto a membrane for probe detection: Southern for DNA, Northern for RNA, Western for protein.
The degree to which a genotype shows its phenotype in an individual, so people with the same mutation can be mildly or severely affected.
Describing an influence on conduction velocity through the heart, particularly the AV node. Sympathetic input is positively dromotropic and parasympathetic is negatively dromotropic.
The strength of cardiac muscle contraction independent of preload or afterload. Positive inotropes include digoxin and sympathetic stimulation.
Peeling off of the outer skin layer in sheets or flakes, as in the desquamating rash of Kawasaki disease or toxic shock syndrome.
Relating to the area of chest over the heart; precordial leads V1-V6 are the ECG leads placed across the chest.
In Ebstein anomaly, the downward displacement of tricuspid leaflets so a portion of the right ventricle functions with atrial pressures and is thin walled.
A mass of platelets, fibrin and microorganisms on a heart valve in infective endocarditis. Fragments can embolize to the brain, spleen and kidneys.
Thin, linear dark streaks under the nail from small bleeds in the nail bed; classic in infective endocarditis but also seen after trauma.
A drug or agent that raises blood pressure by vasoconstriction, such as norepinephrine or vasopressin.
An enzyme inhibitor that binds a site other than the active site, lowering Vmax without changing Km, and cannot be overcome by adding substrate.
The process where a kinase phosphorylates itself, as when ligand binding activates a receptor tyrosine kinase such as the insulin receptor.
Abnormally low oxygen level in arterial blood (PaO2 below 60 mmHg), caused by hypoventilation, V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion limitation or low inspired oxygen.
Around the portal triad of the liver lobule. Periportal hepatocytes (zone 1) are most exposed to oxygenated blood and are affected first in viral hepatitis.
An area that appears darker than normal on x-ray because it absorbs fewer x-rays, as with air in emphysema or lytic bone lesions.
Fluid in the lung from increased capillary permeability rather than high hydrostatic pressure, as in ARDS, with a normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure.
An abnormally loud, low-pitched sound on percussion over air-filled lungs, as in pneumothorax or emphysema.
A blood product made from thawed plasma, rich in fibrinogen, factor VIII, factor XIII and von Willebrand factor, used in DIC and fibrinogen deficiency.
Promoting blood clotting. Examples include thrombin, thromboxane A2 and tissue factor.
Air cells within the ethmoid bone between the eyes and nose. Infection can spread into the orbit, causing orbital cellulitis.
Combined forward curve and lateral curve of the spine, causing restrictive lung disease and hypoventilation when severe.
One half of the chest; for example, complete opacification of a hemithorax on x-ray suggests large effusion or lung collapse.
A stage of lung development (weeks 5 to 17) where the bronchial tree branches to the terminal bronchioles, resembling a gland; no gas exchange is possible.
Delivered as a fine mist inhaled through a mask, as in nebulized albuterol or ipratropium for asthma and COPD.
A neprilysin inhibitor that raises natriuretic peptides, combined with valsartan to treat heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Combining it with an ACE inhibitor risks angioedema.
The protein-free fluid that is pushed through a membrane under pressure, such as the fluid filtered at the glomerulus or across capillary walls.
Passing between cells rather than through them. In the proximal tubule, much sodium, water and calcium is reabsorbed by the paracellular route.
A mass of undifferentiated embryonic cells. The metanephric blastema is induced by the ureteric bud to form nephrons; Wilms tumor arises from it.
Small amounts of albumin in the urine (30 to 300 mg/day), an early marker of diabetic kidney disease.
The supportive tissue between glomerular capillary loops, made of mesangial cells and matrix. It is involved in IgA nephropathy and amyloid deposition.
Enlargement of an organ, such as hepatosplenomegaly; macroglossia and organomegaly are features of Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.
A selective beta-3 agonist that relaxes the bladder detrusor muscle, used for overactive bladder.
A pentose sugar phosphate produced by the oxidative phase of the pentose phosphate pathway, converted to ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis.
The main methyl donor in the body, made from methionine and ATP. It donates methyl groups for reactions such as epinephrine synthesis and DNA methylation.
An enzyme that transfers an amide group from glutamine to another molecule. Glutamine-PRPP amidotransferase catalyzes the committed step of purine synthesis.
Developing red cells containing iron granules. Ringed sideroblasts, with iron-laden mitochondria around the nucleus, characterize sideroblastic anemia.
Hemosiderin in the urine, shed from kidney tubular cells after intravascular hemolysis, as in PNH.
Located before a ganglion. Preganglionic autonomic neurons have cell bodies in the CNS and release acetylcholine onto postganglionic neurons.
Dispersion of Nissl substance in a neuron cell body after its axon is damaged, making the soma swollen with an eccentric nucleus.
Absence of reflexes, seen in lower motor neuron lesions, peripheral neuropathy and Guillain-Barre syndrome.
Crossing of nerve fibers from one side of the nervous system to the other, as in the corticospinal tract in the medulla.
The T-cell zone of a lymph node between the follicles and medulla. It enlarges in viral infections like infectious mononucleosis.
One of the deep cerebellar nuclei, between the dentate and globose nuclei, projecting to the red nucleus.
One of the deep cerebellar nuclei, medial to the emboliform nucleus, projecting to the red nucleus.
A descending motor tract from the red nucleus of the midbrain that facilitates flexor tone in the upper limb.
A brighter than normal region on an MRI sequence, such as high T2 or FLAIR signal in edema, demyelination or ischemia.
Enlargement of the brain ventricles, from hydrocephalus or brain atrophy.
A histologic pattern of tumor cells lining up around areas of necrosis, characteristic of glioblastoma.
The artery running behind the first part of the duodenum. A posterior duodenal ulcer can erode into it and cause major bleeding.
Describing a polyp or lesion that is flat-based, attached directly to the wall without a stalk, in contrast to a pedunculated polyp.
The hook-shaped extension of the pancreatic head behind the superior mesenteric vessels, derived from the ventral pancreatic bud.
The dopamine pathway from the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus to the pituitary; dopamine inhibits prolactin, so blockade by antipsychotics causes hyperprolactinemia.
A water-soluble prodrug of phenytoin given IV or IM to treat status epilepticus, causing less tissue irritation than phenytoin.
Around the nail. Periungual fibromas are tumors in tuberous sclerosis.
A thickened, leathery, orange-peel-textured plaque of skin, usually on the lower back, characteristic of tuberous sclerosis.
Teaching patients and families about a condition and its management as a component of treatment, such as for Tourette syndrome or schizophrenia.
A streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin (SpeA, B, C) that causes the rash of scarlet fever; encoded by a lysogenic phage.
Skin and soft tissue infection without pus or drainage, usually from streptococci, as opposed to purulent infection typically from S. aureus.
A melatonin MT1 and MT2 receptor agonist used for insomnia; it has little abuse potential or dependence.
